name: SWE-Gym
description: The first environment for training software engineering agents, containing 2,438 real-world Python task instances, each comprising a codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. The paper also identifies a 230-instance SWE-Gym Lite subset and releases SWE-Gym Raw with 64,689 Python GitHub issues without executable environments.
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang. Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR 267, 2025.
rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym was constructed from real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests and GitHub issues in 11 popular Python repositories, in close alignment with SWE-Bench. The authors first used SEART GitHub search to filter repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors, resulting in 358 repositories. They then used SWE-Bench's instance extraction script to convert repositories into task instances containing the issue description, repository snapshot, and unit tests, yielding 64,689 instances in SWE-Gym Raw. They semi-automatically associated instances with version numbers and semi-manually created executable environments for 11 repositories. Dependencies were manually configured for each task instance using repository configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation, and instances were validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. After validation and filtering failed instances, 2,438 unit-test-validated instances remained. The process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of Python GitHub repositories and their associated GitHub issues/pull requests. Each extracted instance includes the natural language issue description, a snapshot of the repository in which the issue was created, a set of unit tests, code, and the human-submitted solution patch. SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 Python GitHub issues spanning 358 Python repositories without executable environments.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories were selected from those created before July 1, 2022.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors generalized SWE-Bench's versioning script to support versioning via script execution and semi-automatically collected versions for each instance based on repository information such as pyproject.toml and git tags. They filtered out failed instances after validation and also created a SWE-Gym Lite subset by following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks that require editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, tasks with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Repositories were filtered using SEART GitHub search criteria. SWE-Bench's instance extraction script was used to convert repositories into task instances. For selected repositories, executable environments were set up by manually configuring dependencies using requirements.txt, CI scripts, or repository documentation from the snapshot at issue creation time. The authors then used SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to verify that the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code, and filtered out failed instances. Pre-built Docker images were released for each validated instance.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human effort was used to semi-manually create executable environments for 11 repositories and manually configure dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. The paper states that annotations were done by a subset of the authors. The correctness signal for instances comes from expert-validated or human-written test cases and validation that the human-submitted gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Instances were validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure that the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. Failed instances were filtered out, resulting in 2,438 unit-test-validated instances.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script; SWE-Bench's versioning script; SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors publicly release SWE-Gym, models, agent trajectories, SWE-Gym Raw, and pre-built Docker images for each instance for full reproducibility. No updating timeframe or deprecation policy is specified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries, support critical open-source infrastructure, and potentially make software development more accessible. It also notes possible impacts on software engineering jobs and the need for careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. The authors warn that similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code and encourage future work on responsible deployment, including security, safety, and economic impacts.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes several biases and distribution concerns. Ignoring executable environments could introduce distribution bias and diminish SWE-Gym's utility, which motivated manual environment configuration. The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of the total and bokeh about one percent. The authors also state that repeated sampling introduces a bias toward easier tasks, making training on all successful trajectories suboptimal, and they mitigate this with per-instance capping. In concurrent work comparison, they note that discarding instances that fail setup can bias an environment away from tasks with complex dependencies.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper states that SWE-Gym is limited by environment diversity, including the number of repositories, types of tasks, and programming languages. SWE-Gym contains only Python tasks from 11 repositories, while SWE-Gym Raw lacks executable environments and guarantees that unit tests effectively evaluate correctness. The authors also note that tasks in SWE-Gym may be harder than SWE-Bench and that current self-improvement results are modest. Current SWE settings focus solely on task completion and neglect human-in-the-loop collaboration.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training software engineering agents and verifier/reward models, enabling supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling fine-tuning, self-improvement experiments, and inference-time scaling through verifier reranking. SWE-Gym Lite is described as suitable for rapid prototyping. SWE-Gym Raw is released to support future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis.
